name: BMW M3 (E92)
fuel_economy: ~14 city / 20 hwy mpg (real-world city often lower)
reliability: 7/10 — the S65 is the only V8 M3 and one of the all-time great naturally-aspirated engines, a screaming 8,400 rpm unit derived from the E60 M5's V10. It is also the source of the car's signature worry: connecting-rod bearing wear, which a meaningful share of owners address preventively. Add the throttle-actuator failures (the two units driving the eight individual throttle bodies) and VANOS quirks, and the E92 rewards a proactive owner who shortens oil intervals and budgets for the known items. Do that, and you own the last, most dramatic pre-turbo M3.
cost_to_own: Insurance: High · Maintenance ~$1,500/yr with a rod-bearing job and throttle actuators as budgeted big-ticket items · Values of clean, unmodified manual coupes are firming as the last NA M3
popular_mods: Preventive rod-bearing replacement (often with upgraded bearings) — cheap insurance against the S65's worst failure
An E9x tune / headers to wake up the high-revving V8 without hurting reliability
Replacement throttle actuators before they fail and trigger limp mode
Coilovers and a proper alignment to sharpen an already-brilliant chassis
Honest take: spend on the rod bearings and throttle actuators first — mechanical peace of mind beats bolt-on power on an S65
oil_interval: Every 5,000 miles (well short of BMW's factory interval — owners strongly recommend shortening it)

generations.E92 M3 (2007–2013): The V8 M3. Offered as the E92 coupe, E90 sedan, and E93 convertible, all sharing the 4.0L S65 that revs to 8,400 rpm. High-strung, race-bred, and best experienced near the redline — the peak of M3 drama before turbocharging arrived with the F80.
generations.Competition & special editions: Later Competition Packages added sharper suspension, wheels, and EDC tuning; limited runs like the Lime Rock Park and Frozen editions are the collector picks.

common_issues: Connecting-rod bearing wear — the S65's signature issue; many owners replace preventively
Throttle-actuator failure — the two actuators driving the individual throttle bodies wear out and cause limp mode
Elevated oil consumption (partly by design on a high-revving M engine)
On DCT cars, mechatronics and clutch wear over time
maintenance_tips: Shorten the oil interval to ~5,000 miles with the correct 10W-60 — the single best thing for the rod bearings
Budget for preventive rod-bearing replacement, especially on higher-mileage or unknown-history cars
Replace throttle actuators proactively at the first sign of trouble to avoid being stranded in limp mode
Keep VANOS solenoids serviced and let the V8 reach temperature before chasing the redline
On DCT cars, service the transmission fluid on schedule and watch clutch adaptation values

engine.detail: 4.0L S65B40 naturally-aspirated V8 with architecture derived from the E60 M5's V10 - 414 hp screaming to an 8,400 rpm redline.
engine.watch: Connecting-rod bearing wear is the signature worry (many replace it preventively), so run 10W-60 and shorten oil changes to ~5k; also watch VANOS rattle.

drivetrain.detail: RWD through a 6-speed manual or 7-speed M-DCT dual-clutch.
drivetrain.watch: Manuals are stout (just check clutch wear); on DCT cars budget for mechatronics faults and clutch-pack wear, and service the fluid on schedule.

suspension.detail: Aluminum front control arms and a five-link rear; Competition-package cars add EDC adaptive dampers.
suspension.watch: Expect age-related front control-arm bushing and rear subframe/diff-mount wear - nothing exotic, but a refresh sharpens an already-brilliant chassis.

brakes.detail: Large four-wheel vented discs with floating single-piston calipers - strong street brakes for a ~3,700 lb coupe.
brakes.watch: They wear quickly under track use; watch for warped or heat-cracked rotors and glazed pads on hard-driven cars.

electrical.detail: Eight individual throttle bodies operated by two electronic throttle actuators - a defining S65 induction feature.
electrical.watch: Those actuators wear internally and fail (codes 2B15/2B16), dropping the car into limp mode - replace them proactively at the first sign.
